title: Adaptive fragment-merge strategy and client reconnect policy for streaming responses
creator: Amina Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's SSE-based streaming endpoint is robust but we still see classes of customer-visible issues when clients reconnect during mid-response. Problems include: partial JSON/structured output fragments that are split across connection boundaries, function/tool-call boundaries being split leading to ambiguous tool invocation, and duplicate tokens when naive replays occur.

Objective:
Design and implement a client/server negotiation and server-side checkpointing strategy that minimizes user-facing glitches on reconnect while preserving low-latency streaming. This ticket covers: (1) a server-side stable watermark + soft checkpoints for partial-fragment merges, (2) an idempotent fragment identifier scheme for safe replays, and (3) an adaptive client reconnect/backoff policy that favors rehydration over blind resume.

Non-goals:
- Full durable per-request persistent storage (we will not add long-term DB checkpoints in this phase).
- Breaking changes to existing hosted API surface. All negotiation must be opt-in and backward-compatible.

Design summary:
1) Fragment identifiers: the runtime will emit a monotonic per-session fragment_id and a fragment_seq within each fragment. Each chunk will include an envelope header (X-Fragment-Id, X-Fragment-Seq, X-Fragment-Flags) in the event-stream metadata line. The server promises monotonic seq and marks the last chunk of a logical token or tool call with a FLAG_END.

2) Soft checkpoints and stable watermark: the server will maintain a sliding stable_watermark describing the highest fragment_seq that is resilient to replay (i.e., server-side KV cache + token generation state is stable). Watermark advances when the server flushes the KV-cache and persists minimal replay metadata to the in-memory session store (not durable DB). On reconnect, client can request resume starting at stable_watermark+1 or at an explicit fragment_seq; server accepts resume only up to the latest known fragment_seq and returns a reconciliation hint if the requested seq is non-resumable.

3) Partial-fragment merge: if a reconnect occurs where the last acknowledged fragment was a non-FLAG_END (mid-logical-unit), the server will attempt to merge the re-sent partial fragment with the stored tail using fragment_id and partial checksums. If merge fails, the server will abort the logical unit and emit a graceful degradation event (structured JSON with error metadata and recommended fallback).

4) Tool/Function-call atomicity: tool invocation frames are guarded by a special TOOL_SENTINEL envelope. The runtime will never mark TOOL_SENTINEL as FLAG_END in the middle of a tool payload. On reconnect, if the last recorded fragment is TOOL_SENTINEL without FLAG_END, the server will prioritize returning a resumable token only if the underlying tool execution is idempotent and replay-safe; otherwise, it will return a non-resumable indicator and reroute the request to a fallback variant.

5) Client adaptive reconnect policy: the client SDK will implement a 3-tier reconnect heuristic: quick probe (100–300ms jitter) for transient network blips, extended exponential backoff for sustained outages, and a final rehydration path that requests a full integrity check (server-supplied checksum of last N fragments). The SDK will prefer asking the server for a reconciliation range rather than blind re-sending of the entire prompt when the session is large.

Compatibility and rollout:
- Negotiation header X-SRW-Features will advertise server capabilities: fragment_ids, soft_checkpoint, tool_atomic_resume. Default is opt-out; we will progressively flip on for hosted customers during canary.
- For older clients that do not supply resume fragments, server will continue to stream with best-effort reassembly and will include a deprecation warning in metric logs (no breaking behavior).

Acceptance criteria:
- Server emits fragment metadata in event stream for >=95% of streaming sessions in canary.
- SDK reconnect path recovers and resumes without user-visible JSON parse errors in >=99% of synthetic network-flip tests.
- No regression in median latency for cold-stream start (<= +2% compared to baseline).
- Tool/function-call atomicity tests show zero split-invocation events in integration tests for non-idempotent tool mocks.

Monitoring & metrics:
- New metrics: fragment_emit_rate, fragment_merge_success_rate, resume_accept_rate, resume_reject_reason, tool_split_incidents.
- Dashboards: streaming-resume-health, tool-invocation-integrity.

Testing plan:
- Unit: envelope encode/decode, fragment seq monotonicity, soft checkpoint advancement.
- Integration: simulated flakey network harness (client jitter, mid-chunk drop) with structured-output workloads (JSONL, function-calls) — assert no broken JSON on client after reconnect.
- Load test: verify watermark advancement under 1000 concurrent sessions on a dedicated runtime replica.

Rollout plan:
1) Server side feature gates behind runtime-1.22 canary (10% traffic) for internal customers.
2) SDK patch with opt-in reconnect heuristics (minor semver bump).
3) Expand canary to 50% and run chaos-net tests.
4) Full launch with observability alerts and rollback playbook.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Where to persist minimal replay metadata: in-process memory vs. a light-weight distributed cache? In-process is faster but loses resume capability on pod restart; distributed cache increases complexity and cost. Proposal: start in-process and add a short-lived distributed cache if customers need cross-pod resume.
- How aggressive should watermark advancement be? More aggressive improves resume surface but increases cost to ensure idempotency. We'll tune via canary and a tunable parameter (watermark_window_ms).
